title: Beethoven's metronome marks are too fast. Nobody knows why.

sub: Nobody knows why, and this film does not pretend to.
What it can do is measure what those numbers actually sound like.

a half note is two quarters

lines: Every number measured in DAW Pro.
Nothing here settles it — and nothing should pretend to.

stages.narration: If you have never used one, a metronome is a machine that clicks at a steady speed so a player can keep time. Beethoven got hold of one, and then he did something almost no composer before him had done: he went back through his symphonies and wrote a number on each movement saying exactly how fast it should go. Those numbers survive. And here is the strange part — most of them are faster than almost anybody plays. Not a little faster. Uncomfortably faster. People have been arguing about why for two hundred years, and nobody knows. There are three serious explanations, and I am going to tell you all three and pick none of them, because picking one would be making it up. What I can do is build those numbers in DAW Pro, measure them, and let you hear the thing everybody is arguing about. We start from the mark on the first movement of the Fifth Symphony: half note equals a hundred and eight.

Three words first, in case any of this is new, because the whole argument turns on them. Tempo is just how fast the music goes. Nothing clever, nothing to do with loud or soft or the notes themselves — only speed. Beats per minute is how we count tempo: how many beats fit into one minute. Sixty beats per minute is one beat a second, the tick of a clock. A hundred and twenty is twice that, and it is roughly where a lot of dance music sits. And a metronome mark is how a composer writes the tempo onto the page. It is not just a number. It is a little picture of a note, then an equals sign, then a number. And that picture of a note is the part that is about to cause all the trouble.

Here is what a metronome mark actually says, and what it does not. It says: this many of THIS note, every minute. So the mark has to name a note value. Written music has a whole family of them — a whole note, a half note, a quarter note, an eighth note — and each one is half the length of the one before it. A half note is exactly two quarter notes long. So if a mark says a hundred and eight, everything depends on which note is sitting next to that number. A hundred and eight half notes a minute, and a hundred and eight quarter notes a minute, are two different tempos, and one is twice the other. Hold on to that. There are two more things a mark cannot do. It cannot tell you how long to hold a note that is marked to be held — that mark is called a fermata, and it has no written length at all. And it is one number for a passage that a performer will push and pull the whole way through.

So how big is this problem. Beethoven left a hundred and thirty five metronome marks across his music. Of those, sixty six have been regarded by performers and scholars as absurdly fast, and therefore possibly wrong. That figure comes from a mathematical study of his metronome, and I will come back to that study later. Sixty six out of a hundred and thirty five is not a handful of outliers. It is nearly half of everything he marked. Whatever went wrong, if something did, went wrong a lot. And notice what that already rules out: it is not one careless afternoon. It is a pattern.

Let me show you the trouble on a real screen before anything else. The mark on the first movement of the Fifth Symphony is half note equals a hundred and eight. A hundred and eight half notes every minute. Now here is that same tempo in DAW Pro. The tempo field reads two hundred and sixteen. Not a hundred and eight — two hundred and sixteen. Nothing is wrong. A digital audio workstation counts in quarter notes, because that is what a beat means to a machine, and a half note is two quarter notes, so a hundred and eight half notes a minute is two hundred and sixteen quarter notes a minute. Same tempo. Two numbers. If a piece of software can print the same speed as two different numbers, so can a person with a pen, and that is not a hypothetical.

This is the music. Eight notes, typed in by hand — I have not downloaded a file of anybody's performance and I have not sampled a recording. Three short notes on the same pitch, then a longer note lower down. Then the same shape one step further down. G, G, G, E flat. F, F, F, D. You are looking at a piano roll: time runs left to right, pitch runs up and down, and each blue block is one note. One thing that will confuse you if I do not say it — the app labels that fourth note D sharp, and the score writes it E flat. On a piano those are the same key. Software tends to pick one spelling and stick to it. Underneath the strings there is a woodblock hitting every half note. That woodblock is the metronome, and it is inside the render, not added afterwards, which is what makes it something I can measure.

One honest thing before we go on. In the score, both of those long notes carry a fermata — that instruction to hold. It has no length. The composer is handing the decision to whoever is conducting. Which means that in the most famous eight notes in music, two of the eight are notes that Beethoven's own metronome mark does not govern at all. A DAW cannot express that, and neither can any number. So what you are about to hear plays them strictly as written, which is not how any orchestra on earth performs them. I am not going to quietly let that slide. It is not a flaw in the demonstration, it is part of the lesson: a tempo mark was never the whole instruction, and the argument about Beethoven's marks is partly an argument about how much of the instruction a number was ever supposed to carry.

Before I ask you to believe a single timing measurement in this video, here is the clock being checked. At a hundred and eight ticks a minute, the gap between two ticks should be five hundred and fifty five point five six milliseconds. That is just sixty thousand divided by a hundred and eight. I rendered the click, then found every tick in the audio and measured the gaps. Five hundred and fifty five point five six milliseconds. The widest and the narrowest gap in the whole render differ by one sample — one forty-eight-thousandth of a second. Now, a perfect answer is exactly what a broken measurement looks like, so there is a control. I took the same click, deliberately knocked every tick off the grid by a known amount, and pointed the same probe at it. It found five point four two milliseconds of error where the project says five point four two. The probe can see a mistake. That is why the clean numbers mean something.

And here is something I did not expect, which changed how the rest of this was measured. My first attempt timed the string notes instead of the woodblock, and it gave an answer that looked completely fine and was nonsense. This is why. That is the level of one single held string chord, with nothing else playing, over half a second. It moves by more than nine point seven decibels and turns around about seventy six times a second. A string ensemble is many instruments very slightly out of tune with each other, which is exactly what makes it sound rich, and it means there is no single instant that is the start of the note. So an onset detector correctly finds dozens of rises in one note. The woodblock is one instant. It is in the same render at the same tempo. So everything after this is timed off the metronome, which is, after all, what a metronome is for.

So this is the Fifth Symphony's opening at the speed Beethoven wrote on it — half note equals a hundred and eight, exactly as he marked it, with his metronome clicking underneath. Two things worth saying while you listen. This is a general MIDI string patch, not an orchestra, so do not judge the sound; judge the speed. And this is a repeat of the same eight notes over and over, which is my doing and not his — he develops the idea, I am just looping it, because a drift of a quarter of a second only becomes visible once it has piled up over several goes.

Now, what do conductors actually do. The largest measurement anyone has made of this was published in two thousand and twenty, in the journal PLOS ONE, by Almudena Martín-Castro and Iñaki Ucar. Thirty six complete recordings of nine symphonies, thirty six different conductors, over a hundred and sixty nine hours of music, with the tempo pulled out automatically and checked by hand on samples. What they found is that performances come in about twelve to thirteen beats a minute under the marks, on average. Now I want to be precise about what I am about to do, because it is my arithmetic and not their finding. They measured an average shortfall across everything. I am taking twelve off this one mark, in the mark's own unit, to get something you can listen to. A hundred and eight becomes ninety six. That is not a claim about how any particular conductor plays the Fifth. It is a way of hearing what twelve beats a minute feels like.

Here are both, ten seconds each, twice round. First the mark, then the average performance. The two halves are not level-matched by the software — one gain was set for the pair, so any difference you hear is the tempo and not a volume trick. Measured off the renders: each go through those eight notes takes two hundred and seventy eight milliseconds longer at the slower tempo, and by the fourth time round the slower version is eight hundred and thirty three milliseconds behind. That is a real difference and you can hear it. It is also, and this is the honest bit, not a shocking one. Twelve beats a minute is a difference of character, not a difference of kind. Which is precisely why it is possible to argue for two centuries about whether it is a mistake or a choice.

Let me make that difference impossible to miss, by putting both metronomes in the same ten seconds. Watch the two rows of ticks, and watch the playhead sweeping across in real time. The top row is the mark, the bottom row is the performance average. They start together. Then they come apart by sixty nine point four milliseconds every single tick — and two attacks stop sounding like one event at around thirty milliseconds, so by the second tick you are hearing two clocks instead of one. There is one more thing in there, and it is the chart's own control. At exactly five seconds they land on the same instant again, because nine ticks of the fast one take precisely as long as eight of the slow one. That is arithmetic, not luck, and when I counted the separate ticks in that file the answer was thirty two, which is what those two coincidences predict. One metronome alone has eighteen.

Right. Three explanations, and this is where I stop measuring and start reporting other people's work. Explanation one: the machine was broken. In two thousand and thirteen, Forsén and colleagues modelled Beethoven's kind of metronome mathematically — it is a pendulum with weights on both sides of its pivot, which is a fussier thing than it looks — and showed that a mechanically damaged one could produce readings consistent with unusually fast marks. It fits something real: Beethoven's own letters complain about the device's uneven pulse and record repeated repairs. His actual metronome was tracked down and still exists. And it cannot settle anything, because the weight is missing, so it cannot be tested. This one is marked disputed and it stays disputed.

And there is an argument against the broken machine that you can actually listen to. The Eroica symphony's finale is marked half note equals seventy six. The Fifth's first movement is marked a hundred and eight. Both movements carry a fast tempo word. Here are those two marks as metronomes, one after the other. Seven hundred and eighty nine point five milliseconds between ticks against five hundred and fifty five point five six — they are plainly not the same speed. A machine stuck at one fixed rate could not produce both of those. Whatever was going on, the marks vary movement by movement, which is what you would expect if a person was doing something, and not what you would expect if a spring was.

Explanation two, and this is the one with the most evidence behind it. On the metronomes of that era, the thing you slide up and down the scale is a weight with a marker on it, and there is a well documented way to read it wrong: you read the scale against the wrong side of the marker. The same study I quoted earlier found that forty four of sixty three marks could be explained if Beethoven, or somebody helping him, made exactly that error. And the shape of the evidence is what makes it persuasive. They found a consistent offset — roughly the same size of discrepancy on mark after mark — and a consistent offset is what a reading error looks like. A physical fault would be more likely to scale with the setting. The paper explicitly rejects the broken metronome as the main cause on those grounds. It is one study. It is not a consensus. But it is the most data anybody has brought to this.

Explanation three, and this is the one you can check with your own ears right now. Remember that a mark has to name a note value. What if some of them were read against the wrong one. Listen to this. You are going to hear a metronome set to a hundred and eight, and then a metronome set to a hundred and eight. Those are the same sound, because they are the same setting — a tick every five hundred and fifty five and a half milliseconds, either way. The metronome has not moved. But on the first one I am putting a half note on each tick, and on the second one a quarter note, and since a half note is two quarter notes, the music underneath the second reading runs at half the speed. Nothing about the machine changed. Only what somebody wrote next to the number.

Now the same thing with the music. Both of these are the same eight seconds of clock time, and both are the same number on the metronome. The first is read as half notes, and the second is read as quarter notes. Measured off the two renders, one time through takes two point two two seconds in the first and four point four four in the second — a ratio of two, to five decimal places. So in the same window you get twice as much Beethoven out of one reading as the other, and that is not interpretation, or taste, or a difference of twelve beats. It is a factor of two, from the same number, and it is the largest thing any of the three explanations can do.

And this is not a thought experiment. The single most argued-over mark in Beethoven is the march in the finale of the Ninth Symphony. It is recorded, through his nephew, as eighty four. But the note value was not written down by the person who took the note — it was added later. Read one way the march crawls. Hermann Beck argued in the nineteen fifties for the other reading, which is three times faster, and that is now widely but not universally accepted. Three times. From the same number eighty four, with nothing changed except which note somebody drew beside it. And I want to be careful here, because this is the explanation with the tidiest story, and the tidiest story is the one to be most suspicious of. It is still marked disputed in the literature. It is not the answer. It is a third possibility that happens to be beautifully demonstrable.

So put the three side by side, because they are three different SHAPES of mistake and that is the useful way to hold them. A broken machine would give you an error that depends on the mechanism. A misread scale gives you a constant offset — the same twelve beats off, everywhere. A wrong note value gives you a clean factor of two, or of three. Here is what each of those does to the two marks I have quoted in this video. And here is the honest limit of this chart, stated on it: two marks cannot choose between three explanations. The study that argues for a constant offset used sixty three. This is arithmetic on the three claims, not a measurement of Beethoven, and I would rather show you that plainly than draw a curve through two points and let it look like evidence.

So where does that leave it. Nobody knows why Beethoven's metronome marks read too fast. A damaged machine, a misread scale, a wrong note value — all three have real evidence and named people defending them, and the best study anybody has done leans one way while excluding the symphony with the most contested mark in it. What is not in doubt is the sound. Half note equals a hundred and eight is a real speed, you have heard it, and you have heard what twelve beats a minute under it does, and what happens when the note value changes instead. Every number in this video came off a render made in DAW Pro, the clock was checked against a control before anything was timed with it, and the one thing I have deliberately not done is tell you which explanation is right. If a video about measurement quietly picked a winner because it made a tidier ending, it would be doing the exact thing it is warning you about.

description:
Beethoven wrote metronome marks on his own symphonies, and almost nobody plays them. Nobody knows why. This film presents all three explanations and endorses none of them — what it does instead is measure what the marks actually sound like.

THE SUBJECT IS DISPUTED
Of Beethoven's 135 metronome marks, 66 have long been regarded as absurdly fast. Three explanations compete: a damaged metronome (Forsén and colleagues, 2013, DISPUTED — his own metronome survives but is missing its weight, so it cannot be tested), a misread scale (Martín-Castro and Ucar, PLOS ONE 2020 — 36 recordings, 9 symphonies, a consistent ~12 bpm shortfall, 44 of 63 marks explained), and a notational-unit confusion (the Ninth's march, argued at a factor of 3, still disputed). None of them is the answer and this film does not pick one.

MEASURED HERE
The clock first: a metronome at half note = 108 should tick every 555.5556 ms and measured 555.5556 ms, with a spread across the whole render of 0.0208 ms — ONE SAMPLE at 48 kHz. Positive control: the same probe on a deliberately mistimed render read 5.4236 ms against the project's 5.4172 ms, and on a synthetic train with a known 14 ms swing recovered 14.00 ms.
The drift: taking the 12 bpm shortfall off this mark gives half note = 96. Predicted drift per statement 277.778 ms, measured 277.778 ms; after four statements 833 ms. The two metronomes summed into one file give 32 separate ticks in ten seconds where one alone has 18 — and they land together again at 5.000 s, 9 ticks against 8, which is the count's own control.
The note value: the same setting read as half notes and as quarter notes gives an identical tick and a music ratio measured at 1.99999 — 2.22 s becomes 4.44 s.

WHAT WAS FOUND BY MEASURING
The timing is read off the METRONOME, not off the strings, and that was forced rather than chosen: one held General MIDI string chord's level moves 9.7 dB and turns around 76 times a second, so there is no single instant that is the onset of a string chord and an onset detector correctly finds dozens of rises in one note.

HONESTLY
The eight notes are Beethoven's and are public domain; they were typed in by hand, and no recording of any orchestra was read or analysed. The repetition is mine. Both long notes carry a fermata, which no metronome mark governs, and they are played strictly as written here, which nobody does — the film says so. Taking 12 bpm off a single mark is MY arithmetic applied to a study's average, not that study's finding about this movement.

DISCLOSURE
The narration is a synthetic voice, generated locally. No music-generation model was used; every note was programmed by hand.
